The stretch between full retirement age and the first required distribution at 73 is the last time your household income is soft enough to reshape. Waste it, and the tax cascade that arrives with the first RMD becomes permanent.

At 73, the IRS Uniform Lifetime Table divides your prior-year 401(k) balance by 26.5. If $1.8 million grows to roughly $2.2 million by then at a moderate net return, the first-year RMD is about $83,000. It is mandatory, ordinary income, and lands on top of everything else.

title: Sam Altman Owns 12.2 Million Shares of Reddit Worth Over $1 Billion, Even Though He Holds Zero Equity in OpenAI. Here's Why That Stake Matters for Investors.
detail:
Sam Altman Owns 12.2 Million Shares of Reddit Worth Over $1 Billion, Even Though He Holds Zero Equity in OpenAI. Here's Why That Stake Matters for Investors.
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool
Tue, August 11, 2026 at 10:01 AM PDT 4 min read
RDDT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has repeatedly said he holds no direct equity in the company behind ChatGPT. But over the course of a decade, he quietly built a stake in Reddit (NYSE: RDDT) of about 12.2 million shares -- now worth close to $2 billion -- making him one of that company's largest individual shareholders. The stake is worth watching because it's one of the clearest windows into where he thinks long‑term value from artificial intelligence will actually accrue -- and it sits completely outside OpenAI.

Image source: Getty Images.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Regulatory filings around Reddit's 2024 initial public offering (IPO) showed that entities affiliated with Altman owned about 8.7% of the company, making him its third‑largest shareholder. That block represents roughly 12.2 million shares, an investment he began as far back as Reddit's 2014 Series B round and topped up with an additional $60 million in 2021.

After Reddit's post‑earnings surge in late 2024, that stake was valued at north of $1 billion, though later reporting noted that some of the shares sit in funds where Altman's economic interest is smaller than the headline number implies. Even based on more conservative estimates, this is a nine‑figure bet on Reddit's future as a key layer for information and discussion on the internet.

What about OpenAI?

Contrast that with OpenAI. Altman has repeatedly said he holds no direct equity in the company, and he takes a modest salary to lead it -- a structure originally designed to preserve OpenAI's nonprofit ethos and avoid conflicts for board members. Investigations later revealed he had small, indirect holdings through vehicles like the OpenAI Startup Fund and a fund from venture capital firm Y Combinator, most of which he has since sold.

Yet as of late 2024, he had no ongoing, material economic stake in OpenAI's core entity. That paints a strange picture: the most powerful figure in commercial AI has more personal upside tied to a social platform than to the lab he runs.

For Reddit shareholders, that alignment matters because the AI licensing business has quietly become a meaningful revenue stream for the company. In 2024, Reuters (a division of Thomson Reuters) and other outlets reported a roughly $60 million‑per‑year data deal with Alphabet.

Analysis of Reddit's filings plus Adweek's coverage suggests that OpenAI pays on the order of $70 million annually, with AI licensing contributing about 10% of Reddit's 2024 revenue. Multiyear contracts and remaining performance obligations disclosed in Reddit's 10‑K confirm that these agreements stretch into 2026 and 2027. And talks are underway to move toward more dynamic, usage‑based pricing as AI models rely even more heavily on Reddit's corpus.

What Happened?

A number of stocks jumped in the afternoon session after the July jobs report showed an unexpected loss of 23,000 jobs, signaling a cooling labor market. Economists had forecast a gain of around 80,000 nonfarm payrolls. 

According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%. This weaker-than-expected data led investors to bet on the possibility of an interest rate cut by the Federal Reserve. The logic, often described as "bad news is good news" for the market, suggests that a slowing economy could deter the central bank from further rate hikes, and potentially encourage cuts to stimulate growth. This outlook generally makes borrowing cheaper for companies and increases the relative attractiveness of stocks.

Lower rates are particularly beneficial for growth companies because they reduce the discount rate applied to future earnings, boosting the present value of cash flows that extend further out.

A 56-year-old on Reddit's r/personalfinance recently laid out a familiar dilemma: a parent had passed, and roughly $1.2 million from the parent's 401(k) had landed in an inherited account. The beneficiary was still working, earning a solid income, and wanted to know whether to pull evenly across the 10-year window or wait. The instinct to spread withdrawals feels prudent. It is also, for many high-earning inheritors between 50 and 65, the more expensive choice.

24/7 Wall St.

Under the SECURE Act's 10-year rule, most non-spouse beneficiaries who inherited a 401(k) from someone already taking RMDs must empty the account by the end of year 10, taking at least a minimum distribution each year in between. That framing hides the real lever: when those dollars come out of the account determines what bracket they land in, and the gap between working-year brackets and early-retirement brackets is where the money is made.

Why Back-Loading Beats Even Distribution

Consider a married couple filing jointly with $175,000 in wages. In 2026, the 24% bracket runs to $211,400 of taxable income, and the 32% bracket begins there and runs to $403,550. Pulling $120,000 a year from the inherited account stacks nearly all of it into 32% territory. Across the full 10-year window, the pro-rata approach lands roughly $320,000 of federal tax on the $1.2 million balance, once modest growth is included.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Amazon (AMZN) emerge as the two most viable suitors, with Microsoft offering OpenAI synergies and Amazon leveraging Reddit's high-intent shopping conversations.

There is no announced or rumored deal for Reddit (NYSE:RDDT). But with shares down 32.5% year to date to $155.26 despite 61.1% revenue growth and a $1.25 EPS that topped consensus by 29.23%, the question of who could own the internet's largest repository of authentic human conversation is worth asking. Steve Huffman framed the strategic asset plainly: "AI compresses the internet into summaries. Reddit delivers the opposite: deep discussions, passionate debates, and lived experiences."

24/7 Wall St.

At a $29.9 billion market cap, Reddit is affordable for every name below. The bigger obstacle is governance: Co-founder and CEO Steve Huffman, largest shareholder Advance/Newhouse, and others hold super-voting Class B stock, so any bid needs insider blessing.

Meta: The Longest Shot

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META) has the community-adjacency logic and $1.5 trillion in market value to pay any price. It also carries the highest antitrust risk of any bidder. Adding another social graph to Facebook and Instagram would draw immediate FTC attention. Realistic odds: very low.

Alphabet: Strategic Fit, Regulatory Nightmare

Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOGL) already licenses Reddit data for Gemini and drives a meaningful share of referral traffic. Sundar Pichai has said, "Our AI investments are redefining what's possible across every part of our business." But with the DOJ Search remedies still active, owning the site that trains its rival's models is a regulatory non-starter. A deeper licensing deal is far more likely than an acquisition.

Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), at a $2.9 trillion cap, has the cleanest commercial rationale. Reddit's high-intent shopping conversations, the newly generally available Shopify integration, and the roughly half of U.S. shoppers who verify AI recommendations on Reddit before buying feed directly into Amazon's ad business, which reached $19.8 billion last quarter. Antitrust risk is moderate but manageable.

Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA) converts 401(k) employer stock gains into long-term capital gains, saving Diane $112,000 versus a standard IRA rollover.

NUA taxes only the $140,000 cost basis as ordinary income now, while $560,000 in appreciation is later taxed at just 15%.

The entire 401(k) must be distributed within one tax year or the NUA election is permanently and irrevocably lost.

A Reddit thread in r/Fire earlier this year followed a laid-off medical-device VP staring at a $480,000 severance offer and a 401(k) stuffed with employer stock she had accumulated over 22 years. Her question was the same one every senior operator asks when a termination letter lands: how do I keep the IRS from taking a third of my payout, and what do I do with the company shares sitting inside my retirement plan?

24/7 Wall St.

The answer for her, and for a hypothetical 56-year-old executive we will call Diane, was Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA), a rarely used 401(k) provision that turns ordinary income into long-term capital gains at the moment of separation and is often overlooked in favor of a Roth conversion or the Rule of 55.

The Setup: Severance, Company Stock, and a Closing Window

Diane, 56, was let go in a restructuring. Her package: $480,000 in severance paid across 2026, pushing her taxable income into the 35% federal bracket that begins at $256,225 for single filers. Her 401(k) held $1.6 million, of which $700,000 was employer stock she had bought inside the plan for a cost basis of $140,000. The remaining $560,000 was pure appreciation.

The default move (the one most departing executives make) is to roll the entire 401(k) into an IRA. Simple, tidy, and it turns every future dollar withdrawn (including that $560,000 of company-stock gain) into ordinary income. At a blended 32% to 35% marginal rate during her drawdown years, that appreciation would eventually cost her north of $180,000 in federal tax.
